note.text: Quantifiers express amounts or numbers. Many and a few commonly go with plural countable nouns; much and a little with uncountable nouns. Some and a lot of can work with both, subject to context. A few suggests some, whereas few emphasises not many; a little suggests some, whereas little emphasises a shortage. Use the noun's meaning in context: paper as a material differs from papers as documents. Avoid treating all nouns as countable merely because they refer to real objects.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: Quantifiers express amounts or numbers. Many and a few commonly go with plural countable nouns; much and a little with uncountable nouns. Some and a lot of can work with both, subject to context. A few suggests some, whereas few emphasises not many; a little suggests some, whereas little emphasises a shortage. Use the noun's meaning in context: paper as a material differs from papers as documents. Avoid treating all nouns as countable merely because they refer to real objects.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: The club has a few books and a little time. It does not have much money, but many members can help. This uses books and members as countable, money and time as uncountable in these sentences. Changing a few to few can change the writer's emphasis even when both sentences are grammatical.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify the noun and decide how it is being used. Choose the quantifier that fits both its countability and the intended emphasis. Check the rest of the sentence rather than accepting a word just because it is familiar.
